title: Semantic & KV Prompt Caching for Low-Latency LLM Inference

spark.summary: Combining L1 exact-hash + L2 HNSW semantic response caching (with cross-encoder verification) and L3 RadixAttention KV-prefix caching eliminates redundant LLM prefill and decode compute, cutting hit latency to < 15 ms and TTFT by 80%+.
spark.keyTakeaway: Semantic caching bypasses the LLM entirely on paraphrased queries (cos >= 0.94 + cross-encoder guard), while KV prompt caching reuses precomputed attention states for shared system prompts and RAG context on cache misses.
spark.byteSummary:
LLM inference is bottlenecked by two distinct costs: compute-bound prefill over long system/RAG prompts (driving Time-to-First-Token) and memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive decode. A unified caching strategy attacks both layers.

At the response layer, L1 exact SHA-256 hash lookup and L2 HNSW vector similarity search (over normalized MiniLM/BGE query embeddings) detect repeated or paraphrased questions. Because raw cosine similarity can conflate near-opposite queries ('cancel my order' vs. 'confirm my order'), a lightweight cross-encoder or NLI gate verifies semantic equivalence before serving a cached completion in < 15 ms.

When a query is genuinely novel (cache miss), L3 KV Prompt Caching (such as SGLang RadixAttention or vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching) matches shared token prefixes (system instructions, few-shot examples, tool schemas) in a radix tree of paged KV blocks—skipping redundant prefill and cutting TTFT by 80%+.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: Response Caching vs. Prefix KV Caching
learningJourney.purpose: Distinguish full-response semantic caching (skips entire LLM) from KV prompt caching (skips prefill on misses).
learningJourney.explanation: Semantic caching stores `(query_embedding, prompt_metadata) -> final_completion` and bypasses GPU inference completely on hits. KV prompt caching operates inside the inference engine, storing precomputed Key/Value attention tensors for shared prompt prefixes so novel user suffixes skip O(N^2) prefill computation.

sectionDiagram.title: Response Bypass (L1/L2) vs. Prefill Reuse (L3 KV Prefix)

cards.label: 100% Cost Avoidance
cards.detail: L1/L2 hits consume zero GPU FLOPs and return in 10-15 ms.

cards.label: 80%+ TTFT Reduction
cards.detail: L3 prefix KV reuse skips prefilling 8K-32K system/RAG tokens on cache misses.

sectionDiagram.summary: L1/L2 response caches bypass GPU inference on repeated intents, while L3 KV prefix caches skip redundant prefill on novel queries.
sectionDiagram.caption: L1/L2 response caching bypasses the LLM on hits, while L3 KV prefix caching skips prefill on misses.

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: L1 Exact Hash & Canonical Prompt Normalization
learningJourney.purpose: Capture deterministic repeats in < 1 ms using canonicalized SHA-256 keys scoped by tenant and model version.
learningJourney.explanation: Before spending embedding FLOPs, an L1 Redis/Valkey lookup checks `SHA256(tenant_id || model_id || temperature || canonical_messages)`. Normalizing whitespace and stripping volatile trace IDs boosts L1 hit rates without risking cross-tenant leaks or stale model-version responses.

sectionDiagram.title: Tenant-Scoped Canonical SHA-256 Lookup in < 1 ms

cards.label: Temperature Guard
cards.detail: High-temperature creative prompts (temp > 0.3) are typically bypassed or keyed separately to preserve diversity.

cards.label: Tenant Isolation
cards.detail: Prefixing every key with tenant_id and RBAC policy hash prevents cross-tenant data leakage.

sectionDiagram.summary: L1 exact-hash caching resolves identical prompts in < 1 ms while enforcing tenant, model-version, and temperature isolation.
sectionDiagram.caption: Canonicalized prompts hashed with tenant_id and model_id resolve exact hits in Redis/Valkey in under 1 ms.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: L2 HNSW Semantic Lookup & Embedding Vectorization
learningJourney.purpose: Match paraphrased queries using compact bi-encoder embeddings and metadata-filtered HNSW search.
learningJourney.explanation: On an L1 miss, the router embeds the user query (plus intent context) using a fast CPU/ONNX bi-encoder (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or BGE-small, ~4 ms) and queries a metadata-filtered HNSW index scoped to `tenant_id` and `model_id`. Candidates with cosine similarity >= 0.94 advance to verification.

sectionDiagram.title: 4 ms ONNX Embedding + Tenant-Filtered HNSW Candidate Search

cards.label: Pre-Filtered HNSW
cards.detail: Filtering by tenant_id inside HNSW traversal prevents empty results when another tenant dominates Top-K.

cards.label: 384-D Speed
cards.detail: Compact 384-D embeddings keep ONNX inference under 5 ms on CPU and shrink HNSW RAM by 4x vs 1536-D.

sectionDiagram.summary: L2 semantic search embeds queries in ~4 ms and runs tenant-filtered HNSW ANN lookup for candidates >= 0.94 cosine similarity.
sectionDiagram.caption: ONNX MiniLM embedding and tenant-filtered HNSW retrieval surface semantic cache candidates in ~7 ms.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Cross-Encoder False-Positive Guard
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent dangerous semantic cache collisions on negated, numeric, or entity-swapped queries.
learningJourney.explanation: Bi-encoder cosine similarity frequently scores 'Transfer $100 to Alice' and 'Transfer $1000 to Bob' (or 'enable MFA' vs. 'disable MFA') above 0.94. Passing Top-1/Top-3 HNSW hits through a fast cross-encoder / entity-diff gate (e.g., 5 ms) catches polarity flips, number mismatches, and entity swaps before serving.
learningJourney.codeExample:
import re

def entity_and_number_guard(query_a: str, query_b: str, cross_encoder_score: float, min_ce: float = 0.90) -> bool:
    nums_a = re.findall(r'\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b', query_a)
    nums_b = re.findall(r'\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b', query_b)
    if nums_a != nums_b:
        return False
    return cross_encoder_score >= min_ce

sectionDiagram.title: Entity/Numeric Parity + Cross-Encoder Equivalence Verification

cards.label: Zero Polarity Bugs
cards.detail: Full cross-attention catches single-word negations ('not', 'disable', 'cancel') that pooling erases.

cards.label: Numeric Invariant
cards.detail: Exact regex parity on numbers, dates, and UUIDs guarantees no wrong-amount cache hits.

sectionDiagram.summary: Numeric/entity parity checks and a 5 ms cross-encoder gate block false-positive semantic hits on negations or changed parameters.
sectionDiagram.caption: Numeric parity checks and a cross-encoder equivalence gate block dangerous semantic cache false positives.

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: L3 RadixAttention KV-Cache Prefix Trees
learningJourney.purpose: Reuse precomputed Key/Value attention tensors across requests sharing system prompts, tools, or RAG documents.
learningJourney.explanation: When L1/L2 miss, L3 prefix caching inside vLLM/SGLang organizes token sequences into a compressed Radix Tree whose edges point to paged KV-cache blocks in GPU HBM and host DRAM. Matching a 4,096-token system+RAG prefix skips prefilling those 4,096 tokens, computing attention only over the new 64-token user question.

sectionDiagram.title: RadixAttention Prefix Tree Mapping Token Chains to Paged KV Blocks

cards.label: HBM -> DRAM Offload
cards.detail: Cold KV blocks are evicted from GPU HBM to host DRAM (LMCache/Mooncake) before deletion, expanding prefix capacity 10x.

cards.label: LRU Eviction
cards.detail: Leaf nodes in the radix tree with refcount == 0 are evicted first under HBM pressure.

sectionDiagram.summary: RadixAttention matches shared prompt prefixes in O(prefix_len) to reuse paged KV blocks and slash TTFT by 80%+.
sectionDiagram.caption: RadixAttention matches shared 4096-token prefixes to pinned KV blocks, prefilling only the 64-token user suffix.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: Prefix-Aware Consistent Hash Routing
learningJourney.purpose: Route cache misses to the specific GPU replica that already holds the warm KV prefix blocks in HBM.
learningJourney.explanation: If round-robin load balancing sprays requests for the same 8K-token agent system prompt across 32 GPU workers, L3 KV cache hit rates drop to 1/32 (3%). Prefix-aware consistent hashing hashes the first K tokens (e.g., first 512 tokens) to pick primary/secondary workers, bounded by a load-skew cap so hot prefixes spill cleanly.

sectionDiagram.title: Bounded-Load Consistent Hashing for Distributed KV Locality

cards.label: 28x Higher KV Hit Rate
cards.detail: Prefix affinity turns a 3% random-routing hit rate into 85%+ across a 32-GPU fleet.

cards.label: Bounded-Load Spillover
cards.detail: Capping load at 1.25x cluster average ensures a viral tenant prompt spills to a secondary replica instead of queuing.

sectionDiagram.summary: Bounded-load consistent hashing on the first 512 prompt tokens preserves L3 KV cache locality without creating hot GPU shards.
sectionDiagram.caption: Prefix-aware consistent hashing with a 1.25x load cap routes misses to warm KV GPU replicas.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: Cache Invalidation, TTLs & Write-Back Consistency
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent stale RAG/tool answers and cache poisoning using model-version epochs, corpus-version tags, and async write-back.
learningJourney.explanation: Semantic caches must never return stale answers after a knowledge-base update, model weights upgrade, or RBAC permission change. Every cached entry is tagged with `(model_epoch, kb_version, policy_epoch, ttl_sec)` and written asynchronously after stream completion—never caching error responses, empty outputs, or PII-bearing user-specific replies.

sectionDiagram.title: Epoch-Based Invalidation & Safe Async Write-Back

cards.label: Instant Epoch Invalidation
cards.detail: Bumping kb_version or model_epoch invalidates stale entries in O(1) without scanning Redis keys.

cards.label: Zero Poisoned Entries
cards.detail: Never cache truncated responses (finish_reason='length'), 5xx fallbacks, or real-time 'what time is it' queries.

sectionDiagram.summary: Epoch versioning, TTLs, and async PII/error-filtered write-back keep semantic caches fresh and safe without slowing responses.
sectionDiagram.caption: Completed responses pass PII/volatility filters and epoch tagging before async write-back to L1/L2 caches.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a cross-encoder + numeric/entity parity gate needed on top of HNSW cosine similarity (>= 0.94) in an L2 semantic cache?

options.text: Because bi-encoder embeddings can score near-opposite or parameter-changed queries (e.g. 'enable MFA' vs 'disable MFA', or '$100' vs '$1000') above 0.94.
options.feedback: Correct. Bi-encoders compress queries into a single vector, losing fine negation or numeric differences that cross-encoders catch.

options.text: Because HNSW cannot compute dot products on 384-D vectors.
options.feedback: Incorrect. HNSW computes exact or quantized vector distances natively.

options.text: Because Redis does not support SHA-256 keys.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Redis supports arbitrary string/binary keys for L1 exact lookup.

options.text: Because cross-encoders generate the final LLM tokens directly.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Cross-encoders only score equivalence (0..1) between the incoming query and cached candidate.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Bi-encoder cosine similarity alone risks false-positive hits on negations or swapped numbers/entities, so a cross-encoder + parity gate is essential.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens when L1 and L2 response caches miss on a query that shares a 4,096-token system prompt and tool schema with prior requests?

options.text: L3 RadixAttention KV-prefix caching reuses the pinned 4,096-token KV blocks and only prefills the new user suffix tokens.
options.feedback: Correct. Prefix KV reuse skips redundant attention computation over the shared 4,096-token prefix, cutting TTFT by 80%+.

options.text: The gateway returns a 504 error because L1 and L2 missed.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Cache misses route to the GPU inference cluster.

options.text: The L2 HNSW index deletes the user's embedding.
options.feedback: Incorrect. On a valid miss, the new response is written back asynchronously.

options.text: The GPU recomputes all 4,096 prefix tokens from scratch on every request.
options.feedback: Incorrect. RadixAttention avoids recomputing matched prefix tokens.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: L3 KV prompt caching matches the shared 4,096-token prefix in a radix tree and reuses precomputed KV blocks in HBM/DRAM.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does prefix-aware consistent hashing use bounded-load spillover (e.g., 1.25x average load) when routing misses to GPU workers?

options.text: To preserve L3 KV cache locality on warm GPU replicas while preventing a single viral prefix from overloading one GPU.
options.feedback: Correct. Bounded-load consistent hashing gives high KV hit rates under normal traffic and spills cleanly during hot-prefix spikes.

options.text: To disable L1 exact-hash caching in Redis.
options.feedback: Incorrect. L1/L2 caches sit in front of GPU routing.

options.text: To force every request to hit a different GPU worker.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Round-robin destroys KV prefix locality; consistent hashing preserves it.
Incorrect. Vector quantization is unrelated to GPU request routing.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Bounded-load consistent hashing balances L3 KV prefix locality against hot-shard overload.

beginner.summary: LLM caching uses two tricks: a smart response cache that recognizes rephrased questions, and a prompt prefix cache that reuses shared system instructions.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Reusing past answers for similar questions and shared prompt prefixes makes AI responses much faster and cheaper.
beginner.byteSummary:
Running a large language model for every single question is slow and expensive. A semantic cache stores past answers and matches rephrased questions so the model doesn't have to run again.

For brand-new questions that share the same long system instructions, prompt caching reuses the model's internal memory of those instructions.

intermediate.summary: Layer L1 SHA-256 exact caching, L2 tenant-filtered HNSW semantic caching with a cross-encoder guard, and L3 RadixAttention KV prefix caching.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Adding a cross-encoder + numeric parity gate stops dangerous semantic false positives while L3 KV reuse cuts TTFT by 80%+ on misses.
intermediate.byteSummary:
An L1 Redis SHA-256 lookup resolves exact repeats in < 1 ms. On a miss, an ONNX MiniLM embedding + tenant-filtered HNSW search surfaces semantic matches (>= 0.94) verified by a cross-encoder and numeric parity gate.

True misses route to vLLM/SGLang RadixAttention workers to reuse precomputed KV blocks for shared system/RAG prefixes.

advanced.summary: Scale to 100K QPS with bounded-load (1.25x) prefix-aware consistent hashing, HBM-to-DRAM KV offloading, and epoch-tagged async write-back.
advanced.keyTakeaway: Prefix-aware consistent hashing raises L3 KV hit rates from ~3% (round-robin) to 85%+, while epoch tags invalidate stale KB/model entries in O(1).
advanced.byteSummary:
At 100K QPS across multi-GPU fleets, bounded-load consistent hashing on the first 512 tokens preserves 85%+ L3 KV locality without hot-sharding, while HBM-to-DRAM KV offloading expands prefix capacity 10x.

Async write-back filters out PII, volatile queries, and truncated generations while tagging `(model_epoch, kb_version, ttl_sec)` for O(1) invalidation.
